title: Latency pulse: trace notes and p50/p95/p99 breakdown
content:
Purpose
Quick working snapshot of an end-to-end trace sample (p50/p95/p99) with per-stage breakdowns and first-pass hypotheses. This is a lightweight artifact to share with SRE/bench team before we codify a full runbook.

Context and dataset
- Date of sample: 2026-02-26 collection window (100k traces).
- Traffic shape: production-slice 'beta-embedder-v2' routing, steady QPS ~ 600 over 30m window.
- Sampling: deterministic 1:100 sampling of end-to-end requests with trace IDs.
- Cohorts: three seqlen cohorts created from request metadata: short (<64 tokens), mid (64–256), long (>256).
- Focus: p50/p95/p99 distribution across pipeline stages to find long-tail contributors.

Trace stages instrumented
1) request-parse (ingest & header validation)
2) tokenization (tokenizer service call + local token generation)
3) routing-policy (policy decision + route lookup)
4) batching-wait (time spent queued waiting for batch)
5) model-exec (actual model forward steps; includes kernel time)
   - model-cold-kernel vs model-hot-kernel flagged where applicable
6) kv-cache (KV read/write and cache-miss penalties)
7) postprocess (detokenize, reformat, function args)
8) streaming-egress (latency until first-byte vs final-byte)
9) network-egress (time leaving host to client)

Key aggregate numbers (all cohorts combined) — ms
- end-to-end p50: 78 ms
- end-to-end p95: 210 ms
- end-to-end p99: 540 ms

Per-stage median / p95 / p99 (representative; numbers rounded)
- request-parse: p50=3 / p95=8 / p99=15
- tokenization: p50=6 / p95=18 / p99=45
- routing-policy: p50=2 / p95=6 / p99=18
- batching-wait: p50=10 / p95=62 / p99=230
- model-exec: p50=42 / p95=90 / p99=160
   - note: model-exec p99 contains a bimodal tail (cold vs hot kernel)
- kv-cache: p50=5 / p95=20 / p99=85
- postprocess: p50=4 / p95=10 / p99=22
- streaming-egress (first-byte): p50=1 / p95=6 / p99=20
- network-egress: p50=5 / p95=10 / p99=15

Observations and interpretations
- Long-tail dominated by batching-wait and kv-cache interaction. The p99 for batching-wait is 230ms (≈43% of end-to-end p99). Many traces with large batching-wait are mid-cohort requests.
- Model-exec has a sizable p99 tail (160ms) but is not the largest single contributor. Inspect of model-exec tails shows two subpopulations: kernel-cold (first request after model swap or quantized kernel load) and contention-driven slower kernels when concurrent QPS spikes.
- KV-cache p99 (85ms) indicates frequent remote KV miss penalty in long-cached prefixes; long requests with long context (>256) show higher p99 for kv-cache.
- Tokenization p99=45 ms is non-trivial; downstream profiling shows spikes when the tokenizer service returns with GC events (we observed GC pauses in tokenizer logs for a handful of hosts).

Cohort breakdown (short / mid / long) — top-line p95
- short (<64): p95 = 120 ms. Main contributors: model-exec + batching-wait.
- mid (64–256): p95 = 260 ms. Main contributors: batching wait + kv-cache + model-exec.
- long (>256): p95 = 430 ms. Main contributors: kv-cache miss latency + model-exec + increased streaming egress time.

Representative trace archetypes (sample ids redacted)
- Archetype A (short, p50): request-parse 2ms, tokenization 5ms, batching-wait 2ms, model-exec 36ms, kv-cache 3ms, post 2ms, egress 3ms => total 53ms.
- Archetype B (mid, p95): request-parse 3ms, tokenization 12ms, batching-wait 120ms, model-exec 80ms, kv-cache 18ms, post 6ms, egress 8ms => total 247ms.
- Archetype C (long, p99): request-parse 10ms, tokenization 38ms (tokenizer GC), batching-wait 210ms, model-exec 160ms (cold kernel), kv-cache 85ms (remote miss), post 14ms, streaming 22ms => total 539ms.

Hypotheses (ranked)
1) Batching burst coupling: sporadic partial-batch formation on mid-cohort traffic causes wide batching-wait variance. When bursts hit, partial batches wait longer waiting for threshold or timeout. Policy config may be too latency-optimized for throughput.
2) KV-cache miss amplification: long contexts increase KV read set; remote cache misses amplify latency (network + deserialization). Cache partitioning may be misaligned with request routing.
3) Kernel cold-starts and eviction churn: model-exec p99 correlates with recent model variant swaps and memory pressure on hosts that triggers kernel re-init.
4) Tokenizer GC events: a small set of tokenizer hosts exhibit GC pauses; tokenization spikes align with their host IDs.

Quick experiments run so far (results)
- Temporary experiment: lowered max-batch-wait-time from 60ms -> 30ms for the mid-cohort route for 1 hour. Result: p95 reduced from 260ms -> 200ms, but throughput per-host decreased 12% and token cost increased (fewer consolidated batches). Latency variance improved but unit cost worsened.
- Sticky routing test: pin long-cohort traffic to a smaller subset of hosts (sticky routing) to improve kv-cache locality. Result: kv-cache p95 improved ~18% on the pinned hosts; end-to-end p95 for long cohort decreased by ~9%. Observed increased CPU usage on pinned hosts.

Action items (next 2 weeks)
- Instrumentation:
  - Add explicit kernel-load markers in model-exec spans so we can separate first-request kernel-init from normal forward. (owner: Mateo)
  - Enrich batching spans with batch-size and trigger-reason (timeout vs size). (owner: Rina)
- Experiments:
  - A/B test a lower batch-timeout (30ms vs 60ms) scoped to a small percentage (5%) of mid-cohort traffic and measure p95/p99 + cost delta. (owner: Aria)
  - Run a targeted sticky routing window for long-cohort traffic for 24h with autoscaling guardrails; capture cache hit rate and CPU/memory. (owner: Noah)
- Ops / mitigations:
  - Identify tokenizer hosts with GC spikes and rotate them out of production pool until GC settings adjusted. (owner: platform-eng contact: @platform-gw)
  - Add a temporary fallback policy: if kv-cache miss > 50ms, allow direct model-forward path bypassing remote deserialization for that request to avoid compounding waits (implement in policy layer). (owner: eng-runtime infra)

Open questions / risks
- Cost/latency tradeoff: lowering batch wait reduces p95 but increases per-token cost. We need to quantify the sweet spot for service-level objectives vs economics.
- Cache consistency under sticky routing: will pinning cause hotspots and throttling for long-cohort customers? Monitor for head-of-line effects.
- Does the kernel cold-start frequency increase with our recent binpacking changes? We need to correlate with release/cluster events.

Relevant logs/commands used for sampling
- Trace sample extraction: /scripts/trace-extract --timerange 2026-02-26T14:00:00Z/2026-02-26T14:30:00Z --sample-rate 0.01 --cohorts seqlen
- Batching debug: env REDWOOD_BATCH_DEBUG=1 ./bin/runtime --route beta-embedder-v2 --trace-id <sample>

Notes for handoff to SRE/bench
- Priority: add kernel-load marker + batch trigger reason ASAP so future samples are directly actionable.
- For bench team: replicate mid-cohort bursty traffic with partial batch formation (variable interarrival 1–10 ms) and observe batch-size distribution under 30/60ms timeouts.

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducing the p99 tail locally
1) Simulate mid-cohort traffic with 30% long-instruction prompts to force larger kv reads.
2) Inject artificial tokenizer GC pause (sleep 50ms in tokenizer response) on 5% of hosts.
3) Mix in model-variant swap every 2 minutes to exercise kernel cold path.
4) Collect spans and compare batching-wait and model-exec histograms.

If you want this formalized into a runbook or converted to a Confluence diagnostic page, tell me which experiment to escalate and I will produce a templated playbook.
